techniques.why: plain 2-operator FM (ratio 2, index 1.5) -- a carrier and one modulator, sidebands spreading as the index rises: the neutral FM starting point and the root of every DX-family timbre

index.note: the peak FM index: how many sidebands the tone carries -- how bright and rich it is. As it rises the spectrum brightens steeply while the loudness stays constant (a balance stage holds the level), so only the colour moves, never the volume.

mellow.gloss: few sidebands, close to a pure sine -- soft and round

bright.gloss: a full, singing brightness with rich sidebands

harsh.gloss: hard and edgy, the sidebands crowding the top

screaming.gloss: the brightest, most aggressive FM -- sidebands to the ceiling

ring.note: how long the bright attack rings before the tone darkens. Every FM note begins bright and loses its highs as it is held -- never its loudness. Low collapses to a dark body almost at once; high stays bright deep into the note.

quick.gloss: the brightness collapses almost at once, leaving a dark body

medium.gloss: the bright attack settles into a darker sustain

long.gloss: stays bright well into the note before it darkens

detune.note: a second voice offset a fixed few Hz above the first, so the two drift against each other and the tone undulates. At 0 it stands perfectly still (the static escape); higher is a wider, more present movement. The offset is fixed in HERTZ, so it is the same at every pitch -- not a cent detune that scales with the note, and not pitch vibrato, which belongs to the synth.

pure.gloss: a single still tone, the two voices locked together

gentle.gloss: a slow gentle drift between the two voices

techniques.why: electric piano / rhodes / wurlitzer / dx piano: a struck tine or reed body with a metallic attack that fades back into it; ting = how much metal is in the strike, ring = how long it rings, reed = full body to hollow reed, strike = how hard the hammer hits

ting.note: the metallic 'ting' of the attack. this is the single feature that separates an electric piano from a plain fm tone; at 0 the instrument is only its wooden body. the ting fades back into the body as the note is held -- it loses its brightness, never its loudness.

none.gloss: no metal at all, just the woody body

soft.gloss: a faint chime on the attack

clangy.gloss: a hard bright metallic clang on every note

ring.note: how long the metallic part keeps ringing before it settles into the body. short is a quick struck-tine click, long is a sustained metallic buzz that stays through the note. both ends are taken from real electric pianos: the short end is a rhodes-like tine, the long end a wurlitzer-like reed.

short.gloss: a quick click, gone almost at once

long.gloss: a metallic buzz that stays through the note

hollowness.note: the body's character, from full to hollow. low keeps every harmonic and sounds broad and piano-like; high keeps only the odd harmonics, which is what makes a reed sound hollow and nasal. 'tine' is where a classic electric piano sits.

full.gloss: broad and full, every harmonic present

tine.gloss: the classic tine electric piano body

reed.gloss: hollow and nasal, a reed rather than a tine

strike.note: how hard the hammer hits: how bright the body starts before it softens. this shapes the tone, not the volume -- a hard strike is brighter, not louder.

soft.gloss: mellow and round from the first moment

hard.gloss: struck hard, bright and biting before it settles

techniques.why: drum head / tom / timpani / taiko / conga / djembe: a stretched membrane resonating, whose partials are NOT a harmonic series -- that is what makes a drum a drum; pitched = indefinite tom to definite kettledrum, spot = struck in the centre or at the rim, tension = slack and dull to tight and bright, damping = ringing open or muffled to a thud

pitched.note: how definite the pitch is. an ideal stretched membrane rings at spacings that are not whole-number multiples, so it has no clear note -- that is a tom. loading the head with air in a kettle pulls those spacings towards whole numbers until a real pitch appears -- that is a timpani. this is the deepest thing about the instrument, not a tuning offset: the played pitch itself never changes here, only whether the drum sounds like it HAS one.

tom.gloss: no clear note, just a low woody thump

mixed.gloss: a note starts to emerge from the thump

timpani.gloss: a real singing pitch, a tuned kettledrum

strikepos.note: where the head is struck. dead centre wakes only the modes that breathe evenly across the whole skin, which is round and deep; nearer the rim wakes the ones that ripple around it, which is thinner, harder and more sharply coloured. a real player uses this constantly.

tension.note: how tightly the head is stretched, heard as which partials carry the sound rather than as pitch. slack leaves only the lowest ones and sounds dull and floppy; tight brings the upper ones up and sounds bright and taut.

damping.note: how freely the head is allowed to ring, as with a hand or a felt ring on the skin. open leaves narrow clear resonances that sing; muffled broadens them until the drum reads as a thud with a colour rather than a tone.

muffled.gloss: dead and thuddy, a cloth on the skin

index.note: the peak FM index: how many sidebands the tone carries -- how bright and rich it is. As it rises the spectrum brightens steeply while the loudness stays constant (a balance stage holds the level), so only the colour moves, never the volume.

mellow.gloss: few sidebands, close to a pure sine -- soft and round

bright.gloss: a full, singing brightness with rich sidebands

harsh.gloss: hard and edgy, the sidebands crowding the top

screaming.gloss: the brightest, most aggressive FM -- sidebands to the ceiling

ring.note: how long the bright attack rings before the tone darkens. Every FM note begins bright and loses its highs as it is held -- never its loudness. Low collapses to a dark body almost at once; high stays bright deep into the note.

quick.gloss: the brightness collapses almost at once, leaving a dark body

medium.gloss: the bright attack settles into a darker sustain

long.gloss: stays bright well into the note before it darkens

detune.note: a second voice offset a fixed few Hz above the first, so the two drift against each other and the tone undulates. At 0 it stands perfectly still (the static escape); higher is a wider, more present movement. The offset is fixed in HERTZ, so it is the same at every pitch -- not a cent detune that scales with the note, and not pitch vibrato, which belongs to the synth.

pure.gloss: a single still tone, the two voices locked together

gentle.gloss: a slow gentle drift between the two voices

techniques.why: a wire under tension, plucked once and then left alone: the note is made by the pluck and nothing feeds it afterwards, so it rings and dies the way a real wire does -- long and singing at the bottom of the keyboard, a short bright tick at the top. This is NOT `string`, which is a comb resonator fed the whole time so that a held note stands; it is the other thing, an actual travelling wave in a wire, and it is the only entry in the library that fades by itself. Karplus-Strong with the Jaffe-Smith extensions (David A. Jaffe and Julius O. Smith, 'Extensions of the Karplus-Strong Plucked-String Algorithm', Computer Music Journal 7(2), 1983), as Csound's `wgpluck2` implements it: two delay rails with a one-pole reflection filter standing in for the bridge. THREE THINGS TO KNOW BEFORE REACHING FOR IT. (1) IT TAKES THE KEY AT THE START OF THE NOTE AND THEN HOLDS IT. `wgpluck2` reads its frequency at i-rate, so the `reinit` on `ktrig` in the code is what makes it play the note at all -- and glide, pitch bend, vibrato and everything else on the pitch bus do not reach it once the note has begun. A legato slide leaves the wire at the pitch it was plucked at. A note that has to bend needs a pitch-following body beside it via `+`. (2) IT DECAYS, and how fast depends steeply on the pitch. Measured at the oscillator's default 4x oversampling, time to fall 20 dB: at refl 0.70 a note at 110 and 220 Hz has still not dropped 20 dB after 25 seconds, 440 Hz takes 4.4 s and 880 Hz 0.54 s; at refl 0.85 that is 8.5 s at 220, 1.05 s at 440 and 0.14 s at 880. So a long held note in the top octave will have gone silent by itself while the key is still down. That is the wire, not a fault -- but it is why this entry does not answer a prompt that asks for a sustained tone. The ring length also follows the LRO's oversampling setting, and steeply: at 1x that same 440 Hz note is down in 0.18 s where 4x gives 2.3 s. The model grows its delay line by whole periods until it holds at least 512 samples and rescales the reflection to match, so a shorter line -- a lower rate or a higher note -- ends up with a lossier bridge. It cannot be undone from outside: unwinding that rescaling would need a reflection below zero, which the model does not accept. Every figure here is at the default. (3) IT PLAYS SLIGHTLY FLAT, more so the higher the note and the higher refl. The bridge filter's pole is refl itself, so raising it adds delay to the loop, and the loop's length is the pitch; the delay line is also truncated to whole samples, which bites harder the shorter it is. Measured across the axis: within 4 cents at 110 and 220 Hz, within 18 at 440, and up to 44 cents flat at 880. The mechanism is read off the model's own source; the size of it is not derived, it is declared, and that is why the axis stops at 0.85. ABOVE THE AXIS IS COLOUR, NOT A NOTE. refl 0.90 to 0.98 is a different thing altogether: at 0.98 the sound is gone in 0.17 s at 220 Hz and sits 91 cents flat there, 172 cents at 440. What is left is a crackle, a small dry transient. Worth having -- layered under a pitched body with `+`, never asked to carry the pitch. THE PICKUP POINT IS THE SECOND AXIS. `pick` is where along the wire the sound is heard, and it is real geometry: a harmonic whose still point falls on that spot is simply missing. At 220 Hz, read over the first half-second because the note is already dying after that, the second harmonic runs from -7.0 dB below the fundamental at 0.25 to -11.0 at 0.35, and the third drops into a 68 dB hole at 0.33 -- wiry, then reedy, then round. It moves the LEVEL as well, and the body declares that instead of hiding it (`; LOUDNESS: pick`): across the axis the peak falls 1.25 dB while the note's settled energy RISES 1.75, in opposite directions, and the peak moves by the same amount at every register (-1.24 to -1.25 dB from 55 to 1760 Hz). What travels is the distance between them -- the peak sits 9.7 dB above the settled level at 0.25 and 6.7 dB at 0.35 -- because the wave is spiky near the end of the wire and smooth further along. That is a pluck being a transient, not a volume control, and it is the case §4 stopped judging by threshold on 2026-07-27. Both figures are `lco_measure`'s own peak and rms at the oscillator's default 4x. THE AXIS STOPS AT 0.35 FOR MOVEMENT, NOT FOR LOUDNESS. Raising the pickup damps the colour's travel over the note (46 Hz at 0.25, 20 at 0.35, 16 at 0.37), and at 0.37 combined with the shortest ring (refl 0.85) the body stands still outright when the LRO is run at 1x oversampling. 0.35 is the last point that still moves at every refl and every oversampling setting. Beyond it: at 0.50 the colour stands still at 55, 110 and 220 Hz, and past 0.50 nothing is new -- that is the middle of the wire and everything beyond mirrors what came before, 0.80 measuring within 3 dB of 0.20 over the first six partials. The middle itself, 0.50, kills the even harmonics outright (second harmonic 43 dB down at the attack) and stands still: a striking sound, and a deliberate one -- set it by hand, outside the axis. TWO NOTES ON THE CODE. There is deliberately NO `dcblock`: `wgpluck2` produces no DC worth blocking here (0.05 % of rms at worst), while `dcblock2`'s corner scales with the sample rate, so at the oscillator's 4x it becomes an ~800 Hz highpass that takes 23 dB out of a note at 110 Hz -- it destroys exactly the low end this body is good at. And `PLUCKWIRE:` is a LABEL, which cannot be indexed the way this library's variable names are: a second copy of this body in the same instrument must be given a different label. techniques.why: supersaw / hypersaw -- the trance and rave lead, and the JP-8000's string pads. Seven sawtooth oscillators, one of them the played note and six standing off it. This is a DIGITAL oscillator and that is the whole reason it is its own entry: the saws are deliberately not band limited, so they alias, and Szabo names that fold-back as one of the four things every other emulation misses -- it is what makes the sound airy. Built from Adam Szabo, `How to Emulate the Super Saw`, BSc thesis, KTH Stockholm 2010 (TRITA-CSC-E 2010:131), which measured a Roland JP-8000 and JP-8080: the detune offsets (table 1), the 11th degree detune curve (fig 7), the two mix curves (fig 11), the pitch-tracking high pass on the first harmonic (fig 14/15) and the free-running random phases (fig 18-21). `detune` and `mix` are the machine's own two knobs.

detune.note: how far the six side saws stand off the centre one. The knob is not proportional: Szabo fitted an 11th degree polynomial through 17 measured settings, and it stays nearly flat to 0.5, steepens, then rises drastically after 0.9. So most of the travel is fine tuning -- measured on the outermost saw at 220 Hz: +0.6 cents at 0, +8.7 at 0.25, +18.1 at 0.5, +44.5 at 0.75, +176.7 at 1.0. The offsets are not symmetric and the centre saw is never detuned at all. The beating between the seven is the movement of this body: 2.3 dB at 0, 9.5 dB at 0.5.

tight.gloss: all seven on the note; one thick saw, barely moving

classic.gloss: +18 cents on the outer saw -- the pad and string spread

wide.gloss: +177 cents, close to a chord; the screaming lead end

mix.note: the six side saws against the centre one. Turning it up pulls the centre saw DOWN in a straight line while the six come up in a parabola; they meet at 0.75, not at the maximum the JP-8000 manual claims. Both curves are Szabo's fits to the measured amplitudes. Level follows: 3.8 dB from 0 to 0.75, because six saws add incoherently where one does not.

centred.gloss: the six are almost silent -- a single aliasing saw

even.gloss: all seven at the same level, where they were measured to meet

hollow.gloss: the centre pulled under the six; the note itself recedes

techniques.why: analogue oscillator / vco / minimoog / juno / prophet: ONE waveform generator with every control the shape needs. `wave` picks between two vco2 generators -- the ramp one and the pulse one -- and `width` is the SAME position on both: the fraction of the period spent in the first phase, symmetric at 0.5. So a waveform is a pair of numbers, not a name: a triangle is wave 0 with width 0.5, a saw wave 0 with width near either end, a square wave 1 with width 0.5, a narrow pulse wave 1 with width 0.12. The width is a modulation DESTINATION -- whatever writes it, an LFO, an envelope, a hand, is pulse width modulation, and the measure of that movement is the interval of widths it covers. `finetune` shifts the pitch in cents so several layers can be detuned against each other; `drive` crossfades into a band-limited asymmetric clipper, which puts even harmonics into a triangle or a pulse that had none and redraws a saw that already had every one; `age` is component drift. Level holds to 0.13 dB across `drive` and six registers; across `width` it does not, and must not -- see that parameter.

wave.note: which of the two generators is heard: 0 the ramp one (vco2 imode 4), 1 the pulse one (imode 2), and between them the two are crossfaded. Both read `width` as the same fourth argument, so this control does not name a waveform on its own -- it picks the family and `width` picks the position in it. Measured at 220 Hz with the width at its symmetric 0.5: centroid 675 Hz on the ramp generator (a triangle) against 5620 on the pulse one (a square); at width 0.02 the ramp generator reads 2180 (a saw).

ramp.gloss: the triangle/saw generator -- `width` sets where the ramp breaks

pulse.gloss: the square/pulse generator -- `width` sets the duty

width.note: the fraction of one period spent in the first phase -- rising on the ramp generator, high on the pulse generator -- and it is the same argument to vco2 in both cases. 0.5 is the symmetric one on either: a triangle, a square. There every even harmonic cancels -- odd/even measured 131.3 dB on the ramp generator and 96.5 on the pulse one -- because the amplitudes carry |sin(pi*n*w)| on both (over n on the pulse, over n^2 on the ramp -- the pulse is the derivative of the asymmetric triangle, which is one power of n). Away from 0.5 the even harmonics come in and the nth is cancelled wherever n*w is a whole number. w and 1-w are the same magnitude spectrum, so 0.12 and 0.88 sound alike: measured on the pulse generator with `age` at 0, odd/even 1.6 dB against 1.6 and centroids 4317.1 against 4317.4 Hz. On the PULSE generator a width off 0.5 is also quieter, because the DC it carries, A*(2w-1), is taken out and a narrow pulse is mostly that -- measured 3.77 dB down at 0.12 against 0.5 and 11.28 at 0.02, where rms 2A*sqrt(w(1-w)) predicts 3.74 and 11.06 -- and that is the sound of the thing, not a fault to correct. On the RAMP generator there is no such term: its rms is 1/sqrt(3) at every width -- measured -9.21 dB at 0.02, 0.12, 0.5, 0.88 and 0.98 alike -- so there the same number is colour alone.

end.gloss: the far end: a sawtooth on the ramp generator, a sliver of a pulse on the other

narrow.gloss: well off symmetric -- thin and nasal, and on the pulse generator quieter

symmetric.gloss: odd harmonics only, on either generator: a triangle, a square

wide.gloss: the mirror of narrow -- same spectrum, same level

finetune.note: cents off the played note, so two or three layers of this oscillator can be detuned against each other -- the octave knobs the player has (koct1/2/3) move in octaves and cannot do it. Beating between two layers a few cents apart is what makes a sound thick; that thickness is composed from layers here and is not a knob on one oscillator. Measured: -25 asked gives -25 heard.

flat.gloss: a slow beat against a layer at zero

sharp.gloss: the same beat the other way

drive.note: how far the oscillator is crossfaded into a band-limited asymmetric clipper (`distort1`). The band limit is the point of it: fed the FULL saw a memoryless shaper can only REDRAW the wave -- for a ramp input the output waveform IS the transfer curve, and a saw already carries every harmonic at 1/n, so measured over the whole bounded region of `distort1` every setting takes every partial DOWN at equal loudness. Behind a band limit the shaper regenerates a top instead, which is where a real overdrive's clipper sits. The asymmetry is the other half: `tanh` is an ODD function and can never put an even harmonic into a waveform that has none -- on the triangle it lifts only the odd partials and leaves even/odd at 0.000, where `kshape2` -0.4 takes it to 0.255, and the pulse from 0.000 to 0.161. On the saw, which already has every harmonic, nothing is added and the drive only redraws: even/odd 0.664 to 0.226, centroid 2005 to 2837 Hz. So what this control does depends on the waveform, and it does most where the wave is emptiest. Level holds to 0.13 dB across the axis and six registers.

warm.gloss: a third of the way into the clipper

hot.gloss: all the way in -- the clipper alone

age.note: how far the components have drifted: a slow pitch wander, a jitter on the duty, and a slow level wobble, each scaled by this one value and each at its own unrelated rate so they never lock. At 0 the oscillator is mathematically exact and sounds it. Every voice enters the drift at a different phase, so a chord does not wander in lockstep.

techniques.why: a metal body held ringing by moving air rather than struck: three modes at stretched, non-whole-number spacings, driven continuously by filtered noise whose brightness keeps travelling, so the body never settles and a held note stands. Enigmatic rather than like any named instrument -- machine-room, industrial. Same modal filter bank as `struck_bar` and `cymbal`, but a different body: those are tuned bars and cymbals with whole-number-ish or dense spacings, this one is deliberately stretched and its character comes from the drive moving. stretch = from a hollow whole-number tube to a wide stretched bell. drive = how bright the air working the body is.
techniques.code:
kstr    = 0.475                             ; how far the modes are stretched off whole numbers
kr2     = 2.00 + 1.60 * kstr
kr3     = 3.00 + 5.20 * kstr
kdrv    = 0.40                              ; how bright the air driving the body is
kcen    = 600 * (11.667 ^ kdrv)
aexc    rand 0.05
kcut    oscili kcen * 0.35, 0.09, giSine     ; the drive keeps moving, so the body keeps changing

stretch.note: how far the two upper modes sit off whole-number multiples of the played pitch. at zero they are the 2nd and 3rd harmonic and the body reads as a hollow tube with a note; stretched, the spacings go wide and it reads as a bell or a plate with no clear note. measured: centroid 363 -> 532 Hz across the axis with the loudness holding inside 0.2 dB. both ratios are k-rate, so the stretch may travel over the note.

tube.gloss: whole-number spacings: hollow, with a clear note

bell.gloss: the found body: wide, metallic, no settled note

plate.gloss: far stretched: a plate, all clang and no pitch

drive.note: how bright the air driving the body is, which decides how much of the upper modes ever get woken. measured: centroid 349 -> 526 Hz with the loudness inside 0.2 dB. do NOT reach for the modes' Q instead -- measured over Q 60..1400 that is a 12.3 dB loudness ramp for 56 Hz of colour, i.e. a volume fader wearing a timbre name.

muffled.gloss: worked by dull air; only the lowest mode speaks

room.gloss: the found drive: a machine room

bright.gloss: brighter air, the upper modes come up

hissing.gloss: driven by full-band hiss, all modes lit

motions.why: dark to bright, ONCE: the spectrum opens over the note and stays open. A one-way gesture — it never travels back. Stands on its own (a filter opening) and is also the opening half of the larger movements.

motions.why: a glinting in the TOP of the spectrum: the high partials catch the light and let it go again, irregularly. Only the top moves -- the body of the tone stands still. This form re-weights partials that are ALREADY there, so it needs a tone with a bright tail; on a mellow FM tone there is nothing above the highpass to glint with. The corner is the 8th harmonic, not a fixed frequency, so "the top" means the same thing at every pitch -- and the glint therefore THINS toward the top of the keyboard, where the band above the 8th harmonic is nearly empty. That is the physics of the word, not a defect: high notes have less top left to glint with.

                                        ; must not move in lockstep

                                        ; clamped to the band. 2200 Hz was this corner
                                        ; at C#4 and the 2nd harmonic at 880 Hz.
ahi     butterhp asig, kglt             ; the top of the spectrum, on its own
abri    = asig + ahi * 1.2              ; a fixed GLINTING copy of the tone ...
abri    balance abri, asig, 1           ; ... matched to the clean level ONCE

kpos    = 0.5 + kg
asig    = asig * (1 - kpos) + abri * kpos   ; so this can only move COLOUR
